newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh's father lends moral support to son.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh's father lends moral support to son.

text.p: The father of accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh said on Wednesday he is lending moral support to his son but refused to say whether he believed him to be guilty or innocent.
In a CBS televison interview on Wednesday, the third day of jury selection in the trial, William McVeigh said if his son is a monster, "it's something that's happened in the last few years."
And in an interview with the Rocky Mountain News, he declined to discuss whether he believed his son to be innocent but said his son's story, as he knows it, has not been told.

William McVeigh, 57, has been a daily visitor to the closely guarded courtroom where his 28-year-old son is on trial for planting the bomb at the Alfred P. Murrah federal building almost two years ago, killing 168 people.

He sat in the front row and said he did not look behind him because that was where relatives of people who died in the bombing were sitting. The relatives said they felt sorry for him and the predicament he was in.

During the first two days of jury selection, he hung his head when prosecutors discussed how his son could be executed if found guilty. He also lowered his head when a potential juror wondered how a nice-looking kid like his son could do something so heinous. A pained expression is never far from his face.

In an interview with CBS affliliate KVTV, the elder McVeigh said his son changed after army service and developed a hatred for President Bill Clinton and Attorney General Janet Reno after the government siege of the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, ended in at least 80 deaths.

"If (Tim) is a monster, it is something that happened in the last few years," he told KVTV. In his Rocky Mountain News interview the elder McVeigh said that when the FBI showed him a sketch and asked if it could be his son, "I told them with his views on the government, it wouldn't surprise me a bit."
Most potential jurors quizzed so far in the trial said they could do what the defence called impossible -- judge him fairly despite a torrent of pre-trial publicity.

Nearly all of the 13 people questioned during the first two days of jury selection said they were deeply shocked by the explosion, but added they have not followed the media coverage that closely since the blast.

That pattern seemed set to continue on Wednesday as jury selection resumed with continued questioning of an IBM computer expert who said her Christian beliefs would prohibit her from giving McVeigh the death penalty if he was convicted.
"I don't feel capable of throwing that first stone ... human justice is imperfect, God's justice is perfect," she said. She told the court that she had stayed up all night thinking about the issue.

McVeigh and former army buddy Terry Nichols, who will be tried separately later, pleaded not guilty to the attack, which prosecutors said was in revenge for the federal raid on the Branch Davidian sect.
